title: -μι verbs and common irregular verbs

objectives.can: Recognise and parse the common forms of δίδωμι, τίθημι, ἵστημι, ἀφίημι and οἶδα.
Recognise the -μι verbs and their commonest compounds.

explanation.summary: A small group of very common verbs, whose headword ends in -μι, add their endings straight to the stem. Some of their tenses are regular; others change the stem or add κ. You will meet δίδωμι, τίθημι, ἵστημι and ἀφίημι on every page of the New Testament.

sections.heading: What is different
body: Verbs like λύω join stem and ending with a connecting vowel, ο or ε. The -μι verbs, called athematic, have no such vowel in the present: the ending is added to the stem directly. The present stem is also reduplicated with ι: δίδωμι is δι- + δω-, τίθημι is τι- + θη-, ἵστημι is σι- + στη-, where the first σ has become a rough breathing. Some verbs add -νυ- to the stem instead, such as δείκνυμι.

The stem vowel is long in the singular and short in the plural and elsewhere: δίδωσιν with ω, but δίδοται with ο; τίθησιν with η, but τιθέασιν with ε. The endings are -μι, -ς, -σι(ν), -μεν, -τε, -ασι(ν) in the active.

Most forms outside the present system are regular and look like those of other verbs: the future δώσει, θήσει, ἀφήσει; the aorist passive ἐδόθη, ἐτέθη; the perfect δέδωκεν. What you must learn are the present, the aorist, and a few irregular verbs.

sections.heading: The κ-aorist
body: δίδωμι, τίθημι and ἀφίημι form an active aorist with κ instead of σ: ἔδωκα, ἔθηκα, ἀφῆκα. The endings are those of a first aorist: -α, -ας, -ε(ν), -αμεν, -ατε, -αν. In the New Testament the κ stands in every person, in the plural as well: ἐδώκαμεν, ἔδωκαν, ἔθηκαν, ἀφήκαμεν, ἀφῆκαν. In older Greek the κ stood only in the singular; in the New Testament you find it in every person.

The middle has no κ and uses the short vowel: ἔθετο and ἔθεντο (τίθημι), ἀπέδοντο (ἀποδίδωμι). Compound verbs behave like the simple verb with the prefix in front: παρέδωκεν, ἀπέδωκεν, ἀνέστη, παρέστη. Watch for the augment inside a compound.

sections.heading: ἵστημι: two meanings, two sets of forms
body: ἵστημι has a transitive meaning, 'I make stand, I set up', and an intransitive one, 'I stand'. The tenses divide between them. The present, future and first aorist (ἔστησεν) are transitive: someone sets something up. The second aorist ἔστη and the perfect ἕστηκα are intransitive: ἔστη means 'he stood' (he took his stand) and ἕστηκα means 'I stand' (I have taken a stand and remain in it). The pluperfect εἱστήκει means 'he was standing'. The passive ἐστάθη also appears with the sense 'he stood'.

In the third person plural the first aorist and the second aorist look alike: ἔστησαν can mean 'they set up' or 'they stood', so the sentence decides. Compounds work in the same way: ἀνέστη, 'he rose', is intransitive, ἀνέστησεν, 'he raised', is transitive.

sections.heading: οἶδα, φημί, δείκνυμι and ἀπόλλυμι
body: οἶδα is a perfect in form with the sense of a present: οἶδα, οἶδας, οἶδεν, οἴδαμεν, οἴδατε, οἴδασιν, 'I know'. Its pluperfect ᾔδει is a past, 'he knew'. These forms have already been met.
φημί, 'I say', has few forms: φησίν for 'he says' and ἔφη for 'he said'. ἔφη is an imperfect.

δείκνυμι, 'I show', has the present δείκνυσιν and a regular first aorist ἔδειξεν. ἀπόλλυμι is both transitive and not: ἀπώλεσεν, 'he destroyed' or 'he lost', is active; ἀπώλετο, 'he perished' or 'he was lost', is a middle form; the present ἀπόλλυται is middle or passive.

misunderstandings: The -μι verbs are not rare. δίδωμι and its compounds, τίθημι, ἵστημι and ἀφίημι are among the commonest verbs of the New Testament. The irregularity is mostly in the present and the aorist.
The κ of ἔδωκεν is not a perfect marker. The perfect δέδωκεν has reduplication δε- in front; the aorist ἔδωκεν has an augment ἐ-.
ἔστη is not a passive and not a transitive. It is intransitive: 'he stood'. ἔστησεν, with σ, is transitive: 'he made stand'.
ἔφη looks like a present or an aorist. It is an imperfect of φημί.

deeper.heading: Why these verbs are irregular
body: The athematic verbs are an older layer of Greek. In the earliest Greek there were many of them; most later joined the regular pattern of verbs with a connecting vowel. The forms that remain are the commonest verbs of daily speech, which is why they resisted change. The New Testament already shows some of them turning regular, for example the present ἱστάνομεν, which has the endings of an ordinary verb.
